myths.claim: It does facial recognition.
myths.nuance: Flock states that the Falcon plate reader does not run facial recognition and that none is planned. Flock's Condor video cameras detect, track and zoom on people; InvestigateTV recorded a Condor doing so in June 2026. The statement applies to the Falcon, not to the full product line.

myths.claim: It records video of everyone.
myths.nuance: A Falcon captures six to twelve still frames when its motion sensor triggers; it does not stream or store video. Condor streams live video. Raven records short audio windows. The applicable behaviour depends on which product is installed.

myths.claim: It measures vehicle speed.
myths.nuance: Flock's FAQ states the cameras have no speed-detection capability, and no independent teardown found speed-measurement hardware. Speed is derivable from timestamped frames. Jalopnik reported that Flock removed its 'not used to enforce traffic violations' language from its FAQ in December 2025.

myths.claim: It reads phone identifiers.
myths.nuance: No teardown or document shows a Falcon capturing phone identifiers. Its Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios are documented for installation and battery telemetry. Phone-signal capture products are sold by other vendors.

myths.claim: Only the local agency can see the data.
myths.nuance: Sharing between agencies is part of the platform architecture. An audit log of one Texas deputy's search in April 2025 lists 83,345 cameras in 6,809 networks. Flock told Congress that about 75% of law-enforcement customers had opted into the national lookup. Flock removed federal agencies and three states from the lookup in 2025.

myths.claim: The data is kept forever.
myths.nuance: Flock's default retention is 7 days as of August 2026, changed from 30 days; several state statutes cap it at 21 to 60 days. Agencies can configure longer periods. Flock's Evidence Mode preserves selected data with no published limit.

myths.claim: Flock sells customer data.
myths.nuance: Flock states it has never sold customer data. On 16 February 2026 the clause 'Flock does not own and shall not sell Customer Data' was removed from its terms and a perpetual licence to use customer data was added. Flock describes the change as a clarification.

myths.claim: They are only at intersections.
myths.nuance: Flock's implementation guide and product pages list mid-block locations, highway ramps, subdivision and apartment entrances and business parks, in addition to intersections, plus trailer-mounted and portable Flex units.

myths.claim: It is recording 24/7 and uploading everything.
myths.nuance: Capture is motion-triggered and each upload is a set of image crops and text, not a continuous stream. The sensor triggers on each passing vehicle, day and night, so each vehicle is logged; the distinction affects bandwidth and storage, not coverage.

myths.claim: Drivers can opt out.
myths.nuance: No driver-facing opt-out is documented. An agency can add plates to its own safelist, which affects that agency's instance; reads captured by other networks remain searchable in those networks.

myths.claim: A plate cover or spray defeats it.
myths.nuance: The system records vehicle descriptions independent of plate reads, and 'covered or missing plate' is one of the attributes it indexes per Flock's data sheet and policy documents. Plate obscuring is separately regulated by state vehicle codes.

myths.claim: It cannot read temporary paper tags.
myths.nuance: Flock's data sheet lists reading paper and temporary plates, and distinguishing them from permanent plates, as a feature.

myths.claim: It reads plates and nothing else.
myths.nuance: Flock's product documentation lists make, body type, colour, roof racks, bumper stickers, decals, damage, aftermarket wheels and hitches as recorded attributes, and natural-language search over those descriptions.

myths.claim: The city owns the cameras.
myths.nuance: Flock owns the hardware and leases it at $3,000 per camera per year list price; the agreement requires removal after a contract ends. In Cambridge, Evanston and Verona, cameras were reported installed or operating after cancellation. Cameras on private property or HOA contracts are not covered by a city's decision.

myths.claim: An AI decides who is a criminal.
myths.nuance: Alerts are generated by matching a plate read against hot lists maintained by agencies; an officer acts on the alert. Audits found misread plates in 71% of alerts (Roseville, CA) and 32% (LAPD), attributed to stale or mistyped list entries and OCR error; the ACLU documented wrongful stops at gunpoint following alerts.

myths.claim: The data goes to the federal government.
myths.nuance: Flock states it has no contract with ICE. Audit logs obtained by 404 Media in 2025 show local agencies ran thousands of searches with 'ICE' or 'immigration' as the stated reason, and CBP, HSI, the Secret Service and NCIS held pilot access; the Illinois Secretary of State found that sharing violated state law. Flock removed federal agencies from the lookup and added a federal-sharing toggle in 2025.

myths.claim: Police need a warrant to search it.
myths.nuance: Searches run without a warrant or court order. A case number became a mandatory field in August 2026 and is free text. A federal district court in Norfolk, VA held in 2026 that the network there was not extensive enough to constitute a Fourth Amendment search; the case is on appeal.

myths.claim: Flock has never been hacked.
myths.nuance: No exfiltration of customer data by an attacker is documented. In December 2025 and January 2026, more than sixty Condor cameras and several plate readers were reachable from the internet without authentication, exposing live feeds and archives; Flock attributed the exposure to carrier testing.

myths.claim: It is proven to reduce crime.
myths.nuance: No large independent peer-reviewed causal study has been published. Forbes reported that burglaries rose in San Marino, CA, a city Flock had cited for an 80% drop. Agencies document recovered vehicles and cleared cases; independent attribution of crime-rate changes to the cameras has not been established.

myths.claim: It does not build a profile of anyone's movements.
myths.nuance: Flock's chief information security officer told the Oshkosh, WI council that the system creates no pattern or heat map of an individual's movement. Flock's platform documentation shows a plate search returning every camera that read the vehicle across the retention window, plotted on a map.

myths.claim: Cancelling Flock ends plate reading in the area.
myths.nuance: More than eighty jurisdictions have ended Flock contracts. 404 Media reported that many replaced Flock with Axon or Motorola plate readers with equivalent capability; privately contracted Flock cameras in the same areas continue operating.
